title.analysis: Exact: "The 3 Net Worth Levels When People Start Treating You Differently" (65 characters). The number promises a finite ladder; "net worth" supplies precise search intent; social-treatment framing turns wealth into identity, status and curiosity rather than a calculation lesson. No thresholds are revealed, preserving the gap. It closely duplicates the channel's four-days-earlier Kv9am3AfKN4 title template ("The 3 Net Worth Levels Where Life Start Feeling Differently"), so the two outcomes are not independent evidence for a general formula.

thumbnail.analysis: Actual 1280x720 and 320x180 inspected. Three equal white panels with black dividers and large black labels INVISIBLE / RESPECTED / POWERFUL. The same cartoon man progresses from ignored and sad in a crowd, to a banker handshake, to seated social attention. High contrast, no currency object or threshold, readable at mobile size; the repeated figure and status escalation communicate transformation immediately. The social scenes match the title and script, but POWERFUL visually overstates a portfolio's direct social effect and no saved historical snapshot proves this remained the served thumbnail throughout the measurement window.

script.analysis: All 18,348 stored characters read in five verified contiguous ranges with canonical hash match. Cold open: a bank teller learns your name after seeing your balance; thesis maps three invisible wealth lines and a fourth trap. Baseline contrasts 2022 median and mean US family net worth. Level 1 ($100K, inflation-adjusted to about $200K from Munger-era framing): Rule of 72, compounding examples, paycheck fragility and BofA relationship benefits. Level 2 ($1M): 4% withdrawals, inflation erosion, millionaire prevalence, Chase Private Client and securities-backed lending. Level 3 ($5M-$10M): work-optional framing, private-bank access, social confidence, sudden-wealth risks, lottery evidence and resentment. Payoff: hedonic adaptation/moving goalposts; define enough rather than internalize institutional treatment. Strong circular teller close and frequent rehooks; mechanisms alternate documented products with broad psychological generalizations. ASR is auto-generated and original audio/editing/retention are unverified.

claim_audit: 0:4000 Federal Reserve 2022 SCF reports median family net worth $192,900 and mean $1,063,700 in 2022 dollars, matching the script; it is family/household evidence, not every individual's current 2026 position. The transcript drops a word in the Munger quote and attributes it as direct without a source. Rule of 72 is an approximation; 7% doubles in about 10.3 years, and calling 7% a standard long-term return after inflation is an assumption, not a guarantee.

4000:8000 $100K/$1M/$5M times 7% gives $7K/$70K/$350K gross nominal returns, but "for doing absolutely nothing" omits volatility, taxes and sequence risk. The paycheck-to-paycheck ranges and 44% of $100K earners are survey-dependent and uncited. BofA's current program has a $100K Preferred Honors tier and loan/reward benefits, but underwriting still applies. Munger-era $100K to roughly $200K today is directionally plausible; the exact result depends on quote date and CPI endpoints. Bengen's 4% rule addresses an inflation-adjusted first-year withdrawal for a historical 30-year horizon, not $40K "foreverish."

8000:12000 The transcript's 23.8M US-millionaire count was not reproduced from the latest UBS reports reviewed; the 2024 UBS report listed about 21.95M US adults and newer totals depend on year/definition. Chase documents $150K linked qualifying balances to waive the Private Client fee plus service benefits; that is not a universal admission threshold or proof benefits are worth thousands to each client. Securities-backed lending can avoid an immediate sale but uses taxable collateral, floating SOFR-plus-spread pricing and margin-call/forced-sale risk. The spoken J.P. Morgan $3M/$58K example does not match the current official example ($2M, 5.75%, $115K interest, $25K value for the non-deductible case), making the claimed $148K/31% advantage stale or unsupported. "Never sell, repeat" omits repayment, estate-tax, interest, concentration and collateral risks.

12000:16000 A 4% first-year draw on $5M is $200K arithmetic, but work optionality depends on spending, taxes, horizon and portfolio. J.P. Morgan/Goldman $10M thresholds, $55M median client and 1.6% of households above $10M are uncited and definitions differ between net worth and investable assets. Sudden wealth syndrome is a popular practitioner label, not established here as a formal clinical diagnosis. The Florida study does support that $50K-$150K wins postponed rather than prevented bankruptcy among financially distressed winners; the script overgeneralizes that selected finding to lottery winners and wealth retention broadly. Athlete-loss statistics are correctly flagged as disputed.

16000:18348 Schwab's 2025 survey found $2.3M, not $2.5M, as the average local net worth respondents said was wealthy; $2.5M was the 2024 result. "Your brain adjusts in about a month" is unsupported and too specific. The closing advice to define enough is an interpretation, not a measured universal remedy.

topic.analysis: Evergreen net-worth milestones framed through changing institutional and social treatment. Audience problem: locating oneself on a wealth ladder and understanding when compounding, banking access and work optionality change. Searchable net-worth language plus status anxiety creates broad browse relevance, but thresholds combine liquid/investable assets and household net worth inconsistently. Competition is high and the channel published a near-duplicate net-worth/life-level video four days earlier.
topic.novelty_and_corpus_angle: Original alternative: separate household net worth, liquid assets and investable assets; show each institution's dated eligibility rule and a range of sustainable-spending outcomes, then distinguish observed product treatment from hypothesized social treatment.
